title: Lakewood Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lakewood wells have a 32 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $7,600-$14,200.
h1: Lakewood, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Well records within five miles of Lakewood show a wide range of conditions. The median reported well depth is 32 feet, but the middle half runs from 22 to 85 feet. A smaller group goes much deeper, with the deepest record reaching 1,997 feet.

Reported yields are generally useful for household planning: the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half falls between 8.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Most permits identify fractured bedrock or the Denver aquifer, so a nearby well is useful evidence but not a guarantee for your lot.

sections.heading: Lakewood well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
Lakewood’s reported depths are unusually spread out for a mountain-area market. Seventy-seven percent of wells are under 100 feet, while 14 percent fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 6 percent are 300 to 600 feet, and 3 percent exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,997 feet.

The local drilling model describes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, while many permits name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. That combination makes the parcel’s exact geology important. For a bid, do not use the 32-foot median as a promised drilling depth. Ask for nearby completion records, casing and grout assumptions, and a price for additional footage if the target water-bearing zone is deeper.

sections.heading: What Lakewood wells produce for a household
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half of reported results is 8.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, and 29 percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those figures are encouraging for ordinary household use, but only 248 wells report a pump yield, so the yield dataset is much smaller than the permit record.

Low-producing wells are present but not common in the reported results: 1 percent are under 1 gallon per minute, and 8 percent are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. A buyer should still confirm the well’s permitted use, storage setup, pump test, and actual recovery. An exempt household-use well is subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels in Lakewood are shallow, with no simple trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are relatively shallow. The median depth to water is 16 feet, with the middle half between 11 and 24 feet. That can reduce pumping lift compared with a deep water table, but it also means construction details matter. Proper casing, grout, surface drainage, and a sanitary seal help protect the wellhead from surface water entering the borehole.

The decade series does not show a steady decline. Median measurements were 16 feet in the 1950s, 18 in the 1960s, 13 in the 2000s, 22 in the 2010s, and 12 in the 2020s. Only 138 wells report static water levels, and measurement practices vary, so treat this as local context rather than proof of a changing regional water table.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long-standing drilling activity
sections.html:
Lakewood has a long permit history, with records from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. Permit activity was highest in the 2000s, when 1,504 permits were issued. The 1990s followed with 1,112 permits. The record also includes 729 permits from the 2010s and 472 from the 2020s.

The database lists 6,610 wells in total, 3,547 recorded as constructed, and 3,803 with a reported total depth. The most active listed driller is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 2,109 records. Adams Water Well Drilling (Adams, George E) appears on 125, and High Plains Drilling (Jecminek, Charles L.) on 68. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability.

sections.heading: Lakewood drilling cost starts with depth, not the median alone
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the reported median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $1,600 to $2,200. That is only the hole. A finished well, including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at $7,600 to $14,200.

Those figures should be read as planning ranges, not a fixed bid. A lot that needs a 300-foot or deeper hole will not price like the median Lakewood well. Request separate line items for drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work, water testing, and any difficult access. Ask what happens to the price if the first water-bearing zone is inadequate.

sections.heading: Environmental and building checks belong in the deal
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 466 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 157 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 129 historic mine features. A map does not establish contamination on a particular parcel, but it is a reason to review the well location, historic land use, and available water-quality records before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible, especially where fractured rock controls groundwater movement. Check neighboring well depths, yields, static levels, and aquifer names through Colorado DWR records. Confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, and the proposed building footprint before drilling. If the basin or use requires it, investigate augmentation and other water-right requirements early. Do not assume a permit alone guarantees enough water for a future home.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lakewood, Colorado?
faq.a: Within five miles of Lakewood, the median reported well depth is 32 feet, and the middle half runs from 22 to 85 feet. Most wells are under 100 feet, but 14 percent are 100 to 300 feet and some are much deeper. The deepest record is 1,997 feet, so nearby records matter more than the median alone.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Lakewood?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At Lakewood’s 32-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,600 to $2,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $7,600 to $14,200. Deeper drilling, difficult access, and site-specific equipment can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Lakewood well produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 8.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-two percent of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 1 percent are under 1 gallon per minute. Only 248 wells report a pump yield, so verify the specific well’s test results.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Lakewood?
faq.a: The well records do not establish whether a particular Lakewood well is safe to drink. The mapped area includes 466 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 157 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 129 historic mine features. Test the well for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and maintain proper casing, grout, and sanitary protection.

faq.q: Is Lakewood well water getting deeper?
faq.a: The available decade data does not show a steady decline. Median static water levels were 16 feet in the 1950s, 18 in the 1960s, 13 in the 2000s, 22 in the 2010s, and 12 in the 2020s. Because only 138 wells report static levels and measurements vary, use the series as context, not a prediction for one property.
